title: Biển hiệu song ngữ · Agree / Disagree
prompt: All public signs in tourist destinations should include an international language as well as the local language. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

source.detail: Bài luyện mở rộng biên soạn riêng cho năm 2026. Tham khảo các nhóm chủ đề trong forecast công khai; tình huống, bài mẫu và phân tích được viết mới.
source.disclaimer: Không xác nhận đề này đã xuất hiện hoặc sẽ xuất hiện trong kỳ thi. Các chủ đề ngách được bổ sung để mở rộng phạm vi luyện tập; không gán xác suất ra thi.

keywords: Biển hiệu song ngữ Khách không hiểu chỉ dẫn sơ tán, đổi tuyến hoặc hướng dẫn y tế có thể mắc sai lầm tránh được, gây áp lực nhân viên phải giải thích lại điều biển tốt có thể truyền ngay. Ví dụ tại bến phà, cảnh báo song ngữ rõ về chuyến hủy có thể ngăn khách chờ ở vùng không an toàn hoặc lỡ kết nối thay thế duy nhất.
instructions: Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.
paragraphs: A sign that residents understand may still fail a visitor at the moment when a missed warning or misunderstood direction has consequences beyond minor inconvenience. Bilingual public signs are justified for safety and essential navigation, but translating every minor notice would impose costs that smaller destinations could better spend on maintaining clear local information.

Visitors who cannot understand evacuation instructions, transport changes or medical directions may make avoidable mistakes, placing pressure on staff who must repeatedly explain information that a carefully designed sign could communicate immediately. At a ferry terminal, for example, a clear bilingual warning about a cancelled departure can prevent passengers waiting in an unsafe area or missing the only available alternative connection. Translation here improves the functioning of a public service rather than merely flattering foreign visitors, and retaining the local language ensures that residents are not displaced from their own information environment.

A universal requirement would nevertheless create unnecessary expense where notices change frequently, audiences are almost entirely local or translation into one international language still leaves many visitors unable to read them. Authorities should prioritise high-risk locations, combine short translations with well-tested symbols and provide digital language options for detailed material, rather than crowding every sign with competing blocks of text. The relevant standard is whether a visitor can act correctly when necessary, not whether every municipal notice displays the same decorative appearance of international accessibility regardless of its actual audience.

Bilingual signs should therefore be concentrated where misunderstanding creates serious risk or prevents access to essential services. A combination of concise translations, tested symbols and optional detailed information can serve visitors without requiring small councils to translate every changing notice regardless of who actually needs to read it.
